questions.question: What is the difference between class variables and instance variables in Python?
questions.title: Class Variables vs Instance Variables
questions.direct_answer: A class variable is stored on the class and provides one shared default or value, while an instance variable is assigned to an individual object and represents state specific to that object.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know where attributes live, how lookup falls back to the class, and how instance assignment can shadow a class value.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Saying an inherited class value is copied into every object during construction.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Demonstrate class fallback, per-instance shadowing, and a legitimate shared counter.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Class variables are assigned in the class body and shared through class lookup.
Instance variables are usually assigned through `self` and belong to one object.
An instance can read a class variable when it has no attribute of the same name.
Assigning that name on the instance usually creates a shadowing instance attribute.
Use class variables for true type-wide state, constants, or shared configuration.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
A class variable is defined on the class and is reached by all instances through attribute lookup. An instance variable is assigned on a particular object, usually through `self` in `__init__`, and stores state that can differ for every object.

For example, `Employee.company = "Northwind"` is a class variable because the value describes the whole type. `self.name` is an instance variable because Asha and Ravi need different names. Changing `Employee.company` is visible through instances that have not defined their own `company`.

If code assigns `asha.company = "Branch Office"`, it normally creates an instance attribute. That value shadows the class variable for Asha, while Ravi still finds the class value. Deleting the shadow reveals the class value again.

Shared state should be intentional. A class-level count can track how many instances have been created if updates happen through the class. Per-object values belong on the instance, and mutable collections almost never belong as a shared class default. The deciding question is whether one value belongs to the type or one separate value belongs to each object.

sections.title: Attribute lookup creates sharing without copying
sections.content:
A class body establishes a class namespace. Instances created from it do not normally receive copies of every class entry. When code reads an attribute, Python can find an instance-specific value first and otherwise continue to the class and its bases. This fallback makes a class variable appear shared.

Assignment is different from lookup. An ordinary assignment through an instance writes to that instance, so a same-named value can cover the class-level value without changing it. Assigning through the class changes what every non-shadowing instance finds. Managed descriptors can modify these rules, but the basic model explains most beginner code.

Constants, type labels, and consciously shared registries can belong to a class. Names, balances, and per-user settings belong to instances. A counter changed with `type(self).count += 1` respects the actual subclass, while hard-coding a class name deliberately centralizes the count on that exact class.

sections.title: Where the value lives changes who sees an update
sections.content:
| Operation | Storage changed | Who observes it? |
|---|---|---|
| `Employee.company = "New"` | Class | Every instance without a shadow |
| `asha.company = "Local"` | Asha's instance | Only Asha |
| `self.name = name` | Current instance | Only that object |
| `del asha.company` | Removes Asha's shadow | Asha sees the class value again |

sections.title: Observe class fallback and instance shadowing
sections.content:
```python
class Employee:
    company = "Northwind"

    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name

asha = Employee("Asha")
ravi = Employee("Ravi")
asha.company = "Branch Office"

print(asha.company)
print(ravi.company)
print(Employee.company)
print(asha.__dict__)
```

Only Asha has an instance-level `company`; Ravi still resolves the class attribute.

questions.question: Why is a mutable class attribute shared between Python objects?
questions.title: The Mutable Class Attribute Trap
questions.direct_answer: A mutable class attribute is created once when the class body runs. Instances that do not override that name resolve the same list, dictionary, or set, so an in-place change through one instance is visible through the others.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand object identity, class creation time, lookup, and in-place mutation.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Assuming each instance automatically gets a fresh copy of a list written in the class body.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Contrast mutation of the shared object with rebinding an instance name, then show the safe initializer form.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: The class body runs once, so its list or dictionary is created once.
Instances without their own value find that same object on the class.
An in-place change such as `append` changes the shared object.
Assigning a new value to one instance creates a separate shadow instead.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
A mutable class attribute is shared because the class body executes once. A list written there is one list object stored on the class, not a recipe that creates a list for each future instance.

When two instances read `self.tags` and neither has its own `tags`, attribute lookup finds the class's list for both. If one calls `first.tags.append("urgent")`, `append` mutates that single list, so `second.tags` shows the same item.

Rebinding behaves differently. `first.tags = ["private"]` writes a new attribute on `first`, which shadows the class name rather than changing the original class list. This difference between mutation and assignment explains why the bug can feel inconsistent.

For per-object state, `self.tags = []` belongs in `__init__`; each construction then makes a fresh list. A mutable class attribute is valid only when shared state is truly intended, such as a carefully managed registry. Even then, explicit access through the class makes that ownership easier to see.

sections.title: Creation time determines whether state is shared
sections.content:
A list literal in a class suite is evaluated while Python creates the class. The resulting list is placed in the class namespace. Constructing an instance later does not rerun that literal, and ordinary instances only refer back to the class value during lookup.

Mutation follows the resolved object. `obj.items.append(x)` first retrieves `items`, finds the class's list, and then modifies it. No assignment to `obj.items` occurs. By contrast, `obj.items = [...]` invokes attribute assignment and normally puts the new value in the instance namespace.

Initialization changes the lifetime. A list literal inside `__init__` is evaluated once per constructor call, giving each instance ownership of a different object. This same mental model applies to sets, dictionaries, and user-defined mutable values, and it also explains the related mutable-default-argument problem.

sections.title: Two instances can point to one class-level list
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
  C[Class Task.tags] --> L[One shared list]
  A[Task instance A has no tags] --> C
  B[Task instance B has no tags] --> C
  M[A.tags.append urgent] --> L
  L --> V[Both lookups now show urgent]
```

sections.title: Give each object its own list
sections.content:
```python
class Task:
    def __init__(self, title):
        self.title = title
        self.tags = []

first = Task("Deploy")
second = Task("Document")
first.tags.append("urgent")

print(first.tags)
print(second.tags)
print(first.tags is second.tags)
```

The initializer creates two independent lists, so the second task stays unchanged.
